summary: Round 3, scoped to the delta since b7e295cc9053. The major I raised (the WRITER's pointer epoch unconstrained) is FIXED and the kill re-measured in my own tree, not accepted on the author's word: `new LogKeys(keys.prefix(), 1).latestCheckpointKey()` in CheckpointWriter.writeIfDirty fails theWriterPutsThePointerUnderITSOwnEpochsPrefix, and fails on the KEY assertion (expected .../0000000000000002/ckpt/LATEST, was .../0000000000000001/ckpt/LATEST) rather than incidentally. The carried minor on `written = true` is FIXED and pinned: hoisting `written = true` above the pointer PUT now fails aFailedPOINTERWriteLeavesTheCheckpointUNWRITTENSoALaterTriggerRedoesBoth, on the second assertion, with the right message -- and the injector is one-shot, which the test's own second assertion pins. The Invariants filter is now exercised in both directions: `if (false)` in place of the filter fails theInvariantCheckerToleratesCheckpointsBesideTheChain with 'not a chain entry: bad magic', and so does a narrowed deny-list `endsWith(".ckpt")` that lets /LATEST through -- so both new object kinds are in the fixture, not just one. I also checked the OPPOSITE direction the author did not claim, a filter that skips EVERY key and blinds the oracle: it fails 15 existing InvariantsTest/InvariantsAcrossChainsTest cases, so the narrowing did not buy silence. Rules 4-5: no existing assertion is weakened anywhere in the delta; the only edit to an existing assertion is an `.as()` message, and it is strengthened rather than loosened. failNextPointerPut does not perturb the `.ckpt`-scoped injectors -- disjoint key suffix, its own field, checked in its own block -- and no existing test arms it or reads pointerKeys() under a failure. Baseline and restored tree both green (288 sequencer tests; full `./gradlew test` BUILD SUCCESSFUL), staged diff unchanged at a351aa9e8c7e. One of the three claims in the strengthened `.as()` message does NOT hold, which is the one thing the author asked me to check and the only finding worth carrying; it is minor and does not block.

findings.title: The strengthened `.as()` message overclaims: 'not per request' is not supported by this fixture, and I measured the surviving mutant
findings.detail: The author asked directly whether the new word is true of the fixture. It is not. `commitOne` builds `java.util.List.of(new CommitRequest(...))` -- exactly ONE CommitRequest per commitAll -- so every commit in this test has requests.size() == 1 and the per-trigger count and the per-request count are numerically identical. MEASURED, in my own tree: adding `private int pendingRequests = 1;` to CheckpointWriter, setting `pendingRequests = requests.size();` beside `pendingSequence = log.nextSequence();` in `capture`, and wrapping the pointer PUT in `for (int i = 0; i < pendingRequests; i++)` leaves the WHOLE build green -- `./gradlew test` BUILD SUCCESSFUL, not merely :sequencer:test. Nothing else in the tree closes it either: CheckpointWriterTriggerTest.theCheckpointCountScalesWithDeltasAndNeverWithStreamsOrPods is the only test that varies the number of CommitRequests in one commitAll (4 vs 1), and it asserts on checkpointKeys(), which filters `.ckpt` and cannot see `/LATEST` -- the exact blind spot pointerKeys() was added in this commit to close. So the per-pod-WITHIN-A-BATCH dimension of the pointer PUT is unpinned, and at the cost model's scale that is one pointer PUT per contributing pod per trigger, which is non-negotiable 6. The other two thirds of the message DO hold and I measured both: looping the pointer PUT over pendingStreams.size() fails this test (1 + 3 streams = 4 != 2), and a PUT per entry of the accumulated `pods` map gives 1 + 2 = 3 != 2. Remedy is either the honest weakening -- delete 'not per request' -- or, better, give `commitOne` a request count and drive the second trigger with two CommitRequests in one commitAll, which turns 2 into 3 under the mutant above. Recording it rather than blocking, per review.md: a message that claims more than the fixture can see is misleading, but it does not admit a production defect the way an absent assertion does.
findings.mutation: CheckpointWriter.writeIfDirty: issue the `store.put(keys.latestCheckpointKey(), ...)` once per CommitRequest in the observed batch (captured as pendingRequests = requests.size()). Whole suite green.
findings.failure_scenario: A later change -- or M4.7's batching doing what it exists to do -- moves the pointer PUT so it happens once per CommitRequest rather than once per delta. Every test in the tree stays green: this test's fixture commits one request at a time, and the only test that varies the request count in one commitAll asserts on checkpointKeys(), which filters `.ckpt` and is blind to `/LATEST`. In production a commit window batches every contributing pod's flush into ONE delta, so the pointer PUT rate becomes one per pod per trigger -- a request rate scaling with pods, which is non-negotiable 6 and the exact defect pointerKeys() was added in this commit to make visible. The assertion message says the fixture rules that out; it does not.

findings.title: ManualTicker and tickAndAwait are copied verbatim from CheckpointWriterTriggerTest, and the copy dropped the javadoc that explains why the rendezvous is load-bearing
findings.detail: Lines 55-78 are byte-for-byte the same class and helper as CheckpointWriterTriggerTest:56-86, in the same package, except that the copy omits the javadoc: 'RENDEZVOUS ON THE TICK BEING PROCESSED, not on handing it over. The writer takes from the queue BEFORE it does the work, so returning from tick() proves only that the tick was delivered -- asserting a PUT count at that moment races the writer and passes against a writer that never writes.' That paragraph is the reason the loop on ticksProcessed() exists at all, and it is precisely the knowledge a future editor needs in order not to simplify `tickAndAwait` back into a bare `ticker.tick()`, which would make aFailedPOINTERWrite... race the writer and pass against a writer that never retries. No test is weaker today -- the code is identical and I measured the mutant it exists to kill dying -- so this is a durability-of-the-test concern, not a strength one. Fixing it is optional and, per this round's own guidance, usually wrong; either hoist the helper into a shared test fixture in the package or carry the javadoc across.
findings.mutation: None surviving today; recorded as a maintenance hazard, not a weak-test claim. The mutation it guards against (replacing tickAndAwait with a bare ticker.tick()) is a future edit to the test, not to production.
findings.failure_scenario: A future session simplifies `tickAndAwait` in this file back into a bare `ticker.tick()` -- an obvious-looking tidy, since the copy here carries no javadoc saying why the spin on ticksProcessed() exists. The writer takes from the SynchronousQueue BEFORE doing the work, so aFailedPOINTERWriteLeavesTheCheckpointUNWRITTENSoALaterTriggerRedoesBoth then races the ticker thread and passes against a writer that never retries the checkpoint at all -- the ordering ADR-0034 records goes back to being pinned by nothing, silently.
